term.name: Monoalphabetic cipher
term.short: A monoalphabetic cipher uses one fixed substitution mapping for the entire message.
term.meta_title: Monoalphabetic Cipher — Definition and Analysis | CiphersOnline
term.meta_description: Learn how one fixed substitution alphabet encrypts a message, which ciphers are monoalphabetic, and why frequency analysis can break them.

body.title: Definition
body.html: A monoalphabetic cipher assigns each plaintext symbol one fixed ciphertext counterpart for the whole message. If a plaintext letter appears several times, it is normally replaced by the same ciphertext letter each time.

body.title: Examples and key space
body.html: Caesar, affine, Atbash, and simple substitution are monoalphabetic ciphers. A freely shuffled alphabet has a much larger key space than Caesar, but key-space size alone does not remove the statistical structure of language.

body.title: Why it is vulnerable
body.html: The fixed mapping preserves frequency ranks, repeated-letter patterns, and word shapes. Frequency analysis combined with common words and digrams can recover long ordinary messages, although short or unusual texts may remain ambiguous.

faq.question: Is the Caesar cipher monoalphabetic?
faq.answer: Yes. Its single shifted alphabet is used unchanged throughout the message.

faq.question: Is a random substitution alphabet secure?
faq.answer: It has many possible keys, but long natural-language messages still leak patterns that enable cryptanalysis.
